You are comparing two drafts written from the same brief. Read no other file, and do not run commands or browse; judge only the text below.

Brief: Write the docs-site page for the `release-notes` skill with the sections What it does, When to use it, How it works, and What you get.

<<<DRAFT A
# release-notes

## What it does

`release-notes` drafts release notes from merged PRs between two tags.

## When to use it

Use it to gather PRs and prepare a release draft. Use `technical-writing` when you need to edit prose.

The skill runs only when you invoke it manually:

```text
/release-notes <from-tag> <to-tag>
```

## How it works

`gh` must be signed in. The skill stops if `gh auth status` fails. If either tag does not exist, it stops before drafting.

It skips PRs labeled `skip-notes` and groups the rest by Conventional Commit type, with features, fixes, and breaking changes first. If a PR has labels for several types, it uses the type named by most labels. Ties follow label order.

## What you get

The skill writes `RELEASE_NOTES.md` in the working tree and stops. It never publishes.

Each breaking change needs a migration line. If the PR body has none, the draft marks it `TODO: migration`.
DRAFT A>>>

<<<DRAFT B
# release-notes

## What it does

Drafts release notes from merged PRs between two tags. It groups PRs by Conventional Commit type, with features, fixes, and breaking changes first, and skips PRs labeled `skip-notes`.

## When to use it

Use it to gather merged PRs and draft release notes for a tag range. Use `technical-writing` to edit the prose.

The skill is manual only:

```text
/release-notes <from-tag> <to-tag>
```

Both tags must exist, and `gh` must be signed in.

## How it works

The skill checks authentication with `gh auth status` and stops if the check fails. It also resolves both tags before drafting. If either tag cannot be resolved, it stops with `TAG_UNRESOLVED`.

It then gathers merged PRs between the tags and groups them by type. For PRs with multiple type labels, grouping counts labels using a strict-majority rule; the code breaks ties by label order.

Every breaking change needs a migration line. If the PR body has none, the draft marks it `TODO: migration`.

## What you get

A `RELEASE_NOTES.md` draft in your working tree, with any missing migration lines marked for completion.

The skill stops after writing the file. It never publishes.
DRAFT B>>>

- "overall": Which draft is better overall?

items.title: Thinking
items.text:
I'm weighing the two drafts against each other. Draft A picks the type that most labels name, which is a plurality rule, while Draft B calls it a strict-majority rule with label-order tie-breaking, and those don't quite agree. Draft B also repeats the grouping under both What it does and How it works, and it adds the TAG_UNRESOLVED detail and states prerequisites under When to use. Draft A is tighter, though it puts the migration-line requirement under What, which may be the wrong place for it.

I'm now weighing Draft B's wording: "strict-majority" clashes with its tie-breaking, and it is unclear what happens when there's no strict majority. Draft A is clearer and more careful. For a first-time reader, both get the prerequisites across, B just puts them up front near the command, though A covers them under How it works. I'm going with A overall.

{"reader": "SAME", "careful": "A", "overall": "A", "reason": "Both drafts let a first-time reader run the skill. A is tighter and internally consistent, while B repeats the grouping rules, says \"strict-majority\" but still mentions breaking ties, and leaks implementation detail with \"the code breaks ties\"."}
